newsitem.title: USA: Emerging market debt defies stormy U.S. Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market debt defies stormy U.S. Treasuries.

text.p: Emerging market debt traded mixed on Friday, resisting the pressure from depressed U.S. Treasuries.

The liquid Brady bond market remained remarkably calm as the long bond tumbled after the December non-farm payrolls report. When the Treasuries trimmed losses later on, Bradies edged back from their lows.
"The emerging market debts behave more like true bond now," said Gary Evans, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers.
He explained that recently, Brady spreads tend to tighten when the Treasuries slump and vice versa, whereas previously Brady bonds traded more like equities with erratic swings.

Early in the session, trading sources said, the Bradies were well bid at the lows despite being pounded by falling Treasuries. But sources warned that th ey expect many of the less liquid debts to be marked sharply lower if no signficant recovery in the the Treasuries takes place on Monday.
Reflecting the calmness, option premiums on major Latin Bradies hardly changed on the day, market sources said.
Implied volatility on the most active 30-day option for Brazil C bond BR8D14=RR option was quoted 16 to 17 percent, and for Argentina FRBs ARFLC05=RR about 12 percent.
"The volatility has come down this week," said an options specialist, who noted that both the daily price change and intraday range were smaller.

Even the uncertainty over Ecuador's reform has not rattled the options market. Implied volatility on 30-day Ecuador PDI ECPDI=RR was quoted 18 percent and on Ecuador Pars ECPARS=RR 15 percent, compared to 35 and 32 percent last July on the eve of Ecuador's runoff presidential election, he said.
Jitters over Bulgaria have pumped up the implied volatility on 30-day Bulgaria FLRB BGFLIRG=RR to about 37 percent from 32 to 35 percent the end of last year, the specialist said.
"The bearish aspect is that the (implied volatility of) three-point out-of-the-money put has risen to 42 percent," he added, noting that "skew" showed growing demand for downside protection.
But Evans at Lehman remained upbeat on Bulgaria, downplaying recent turmoil in Sofia, where protesters stormed the parliament demanding a general election.
"The opposition party also wants reform and currency board," he said.
Russia debt prices continued swinging with the latest reports on President Boris Yeltsin's health.
Russia dollar Vnesh RUVNUSLNS=RR lost 1.00 to bid 77-1/2.
"Vnesh should bounce back," said a U.S. bank trader, who noted that the final closing of the restructuring deal would be on track regardless if Yeltsin is at helm.
